The present suit has been filed by the plaintiff for damages of Rs.
3,50,000/- against his own brother and sisters in law.

2 The brief facts of the case as stated by the plaintiff in the plaint are:
2.1
The plaintiff has averred in his plaint that the plaintiff and defendant no. 2 are the real brothers and defendant no. 1 is the wife of defendant CS No. 369/17 Parvez Khan Vs. Shabnam & Ors.

It is averred that due to this act of Late Sh. Munna Khan, the defendants were antagonized and they had falsely implicated the plaintiff in a rape case and lodged a complaint on 05.02.2017 in PS Mahinder Parvez Khan vs Shabnam And Ors on 16 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52199179/

sentences.text: Thereafter, during the investigation in the said complaint, the defendant no. 1 in her statement stated that the plaintiff did not commit any rape or molestation with defendant no. 1 and she had filed the present complaint as there was a dispute between defendant no. 2 and plaintiff over the property.
Subsequently, the said compliant was transferred from PS Mahinder Park to PS Bharat Nagar, Ashok Vihar Delhi- 110053.

It is stated that thereafter, the police officials from PS Bharat Nagar started harassing the plaintiff on the false complaint of the defendant no. 1.
2.2
Plaintiff also sent a notice noted 28.02.2017 to defendants which was duly served by defendants on 06.03.2017.
It is stated that the present suit is filed to recover damages on account of defamation caused due to the acts of the defendants.
Hence, the present suit is filed on behalf of the plaintiff with the following prayers:-

i Decree the suit of the plaintiff against both the defendants and award the amount of compensation / damages of Rs. 3,50,000/- (Rs. Three thousand & fifty thousand only) in favour of the plaintiff, for humiliation and defamation and mental agony which plaintiff has suffered through the false allegations of rape against CS No.
369/17 Parvez Khan Vs. Shabnam & Ors.

It is stated that the present suit should be dismissed.
Defendants further denied the contents stated in the plaint.

10 Issue no. (i) Whether the plaintiff is entitled for the recovery of amount of Rs.

10.1
The onus to prove this issue is upon the plaintiff.

On perusal of Ex.

"......7.

However, as the FIR was subsequently registered by the police, the complaint case was merged with the State case in terms of Section 210 Cr.P.C.

During the said proceedings, 10 had field an action taken report before the Court of Ld. MM during which it was stated that at the time of incident as alleged by the prosecutrix, CCTV footage installed at Chhabra Sweets was examined.
However no CCTV footage of the prosecutrix was found therein.
Subsequently, CCTV footage of the entire day of the alleged incident was checked which revealed that complainant did not come to CS No. 369/17 Parvez Khan Vs. Shabnam & Ors.

10.2 From the aforesaid discharge order, it is evident that the defendant no.
1 had lodged a false complaint against the plaintiff which has resulted in defamation of plaintiff.

The essential ingredients for constituting defamation under tort law are as under:-
(a) The statement must be false and defamatory.

Reliance is placed upon the following judgments:-
"In "Sim v. Stretch, (1936) 2 All ER 1237", it was observed that the defamatory statement must be such which tends to lower a person in the estimation of right thinking members of society generally.

A right thinking man is a reasonable man who is neither unusually suspicious nor unusually naive and he does not always interpret the meaning of words as in case of a lawyer since "he is not inhibited by a knowledge of the rules of construction."
Youssoup v. Metro-Goldwyn Mayer Pictures Ltd., MANU/TN / 0369/2000: AIR 2001 Mad 225.

entities.text: Youssoup v. Metro-Goldwyn Mayer Pictures Ltd., MANU/TN / 0369/2000: AIR 2001 Mad 225
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The plaintiff, a Russian Princess, was falsely imputed by a cinematograph film that she had been raped or seduced by the notorious monk Rasputin.
The court observed that this tended "to make the plaintiff be shunned and avoided" in the estimation of right thinking persons of the society generally.
Ramdhara v. Phulwatibai, 1969 Jab LJ 582.
The plaintiff was a widow aged 45 years.
She was falsely imputated by the defendant that she is a keep of maternal uncle of plaintiff's daughter-in-law.
The court held that this imputation of chastity was a defamation, CS No. 369/17 Parvez Khan Vs. Shabnam & Ors.

sentences.text:
(b) It must be communicated to third party (publication):-
"Publication of the statement does not mean giving publicity but to make the statement known to other person than the person defamed.
For example, if X writes to Y that Z is a cheat, then it is a publication since X has told it to someone other than Z i.e., to Y.
But, if X writes to Z in a closed envelope that you (Z) are a cheat, it is not a publication.
To send something via telegram or postcard that could be read by others can be claimed as publication.
And, if a person knowingly sends something in writing to defame a person in a closed envelope that it will be opened by someone else

, then this amounts to publication;
Delacroix v. Thevenot, (1817) 2 Stark 63.
If an addressee does not know the language in which something has been written to him or he is too blind to read it then what w o u l d b e t h e p o s i t i o n ?
I n a c a s e " M a h e n d r a R a m v . H a r n a n d a n Pd.,MANU/BH/0143/1958: AIR 1958 Pat 445", the Patna High Court considered this dilemma.
The defendant wrote a defamatory letter to the plaintiff in Urdu but the plaintiff did not know Urdu.
The letter was then read by a third person.
The court held that unless it was known to the defendant at the time of writing letter to plaintiff that Urdu was not known to him, he would not be held liable."
(c) It must harm the reputation of the plaintiff.

(d) The defendant must have either known or should have known that the statement was false (knowledge or intention of the defendant):-
"In "Morrison v. Ritchie & Co., (1902) 4 F. 654 (Scotland)", a statement was published in good faith by the defendant that the plaintiff had given birth to twins.
But, the plaintiff was married only two months back and the defendant was unaware of this fact then even they were held liable.
In our country, whether intention to defame is necessary or not, has got different views.

In T.V. Ramasubba Iyer v. Ahmad Mohideen, MANU/TN/0214/1972: AIR 1972 Mad 398, the defendants published in their newspaper that a person from Tirunelveli, exporter of scented agarbattis to Ceylon instead smuggled opium into Ceylon in form of agarbattis and other news was that he was arrested in Ceylon and has CS No. 369/17 Parvez Khan Vs. Shabnam & Ors.

On an action brought by the plaintiff, the defendants pleaded ignorance about the plaintiff and submitted that they had no intention to defame him.

In this case, the Madras High Court did not follow the English cases (Morrison v. Ritchie & Co. and E. Hulton & Co. v. A. Jones),
and held that there was no liability for the statements published innocently.

sentences.text: It was found that the news was untrue and was published negligently and with irresponsibility.
The Court found the defendant liable and awarded a damage of Rs. 10,000 to plaintiff.
If the defendant has defamed the plaintiff's reputation although unintentionally, he is liable.

The words are actionable if false and defamatory, although published accidentally or inadvertently."
10.3
Thus, the present case is a fit case for concluding that the defendants had defamed the plaintiff by making a false complaint against the plaintiff.

The defendants have not come forward with any defence for the action of defamation i.e. defendants have not offered any justification for lodging the complaint, the complaint was not a fair comment by the defendants and the defendants are not entitled to privilege.
10.4 Although defamation has been established in the instant case, the plaintiff has not led any evidence to quantify the damage.
Accordingly, this court is not inclined to award Rs. 3,50,000/- as damages.

However, this court takes judicial notice of the fact that indeed plaintiff had suffered damages and therefore, this court is inclined to award Rs. 50,000/- for mental agony, depression,
psychological challenges, humiliation and loss of reputation.
Accordingly, this issue is party allowed in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendants.
RELIEF 11
The suit of the plaintiff is decreed and the tort of defamation is CS No. 369/17 Parvez Khan Vs. Shabnam & Ors.
